headline: Medford High School to reopen after sewage backup forces evacuation
dek: Students and staff were sent home Monday after a strong sewer odor prompted a building closure; the district said classes, activities and events would resume Tuesday.
body: Medford High School was evacuated and closed for the rest of Monday after a strong sewer odor was reported inside the building, sending students and staff home early. Medford Public Schools said the high school would reopen Tuesday, Oct. 6, with classes, activities, programs and events scheduled to proceed normally. The update, reported by [Boston 25 News](https://www.boston25news.com/news/local/medford-high-school-reopen-tuesday-after-large-sewage-backup-forced-evacuation/JJIVBT4LRZAJTOVVZPJGPPATXM/), gives families a clear next step after an interruption that affected the district’s largest secondary school.

The response began around 11 a.m. Monday, when the Medford Fire Department was called to the school on Winthrop Street to inspect a strong sewer smell in the B2 hallway. Officials then directed the building to be evacuated and closed for the remainder of the day. Medford Public Schools told families that students and staff were safely dismissed, while the district’s other schools continued on their regular schedules. [CBS Boston](https://www.cbsnews.com/boston/news/medford-massachusetts-high-school-dismissed-sewage-smell/) also reported that the district’s bus company arrived to help bring students home after the early dismissal.

A contracted drain company was brought in to locate the backup and clear the affected pipes. Boston 25 reported later Monday that the contractor had identified the backup and that crews were cleaning the sewage smell from the impacted areas. Firefighters remained at the school to monitor the situation. The district’s decision to reopen Tuesday indicates that officials expected the immediate problem to be addressed, but the reports reviewed for this article do not describe the precise blockage, the extent of any water or building damage, or whether testing found a continuing air-quality concern.

The disruption reached beyond the school day. Monday after-school activities and athletics were canceled, rescheduled or moved to modified practices while the building was closed, according to [Medford Patch](https://patch.com/massachusetts/medford/sewage-gas-smell-prompts-medford-high-school-evacuation). Boston 25 said the district planned to hold Tuesday’s activities and events as scheduled. That distinction matters for families arranging transportation and supervision: the Monday closure applied to the high school, while the broader Medford school system remained open, and the Tuesday plan was conditional on the cleanup and reopening decision described by the district.

No injuries were reported in the coverage reviewed. The school district thanked students, staff, community members and transportation partners for following evacuation instructions. The initial odor was described by officials as a sewage or sewage-gas smell, but the public reports do not establish that anyone was exposed to a dangerous concentration or identify a medical cause. NorthEast News did not witness the evacuation or independently inspect the building; the account here is based on the district information quoted by local news organizations and their updates published Monday.

The incident comes as Medford is already planning a long-term replacement or major upgrade for the high school. CBS Boston reported that the current building was completed in 1971, underwent renovations in the early 2000s and in 2013, and is part of a city project that was scheduled to move toward construction in 2028. Those capital plans are separate from Monday’s plumbing response. The sewage backup does not, by itself, establish that the building project caused the odor or that the planned work will change because of the evacuation.

For families, the immediate question is whether the Tuesday reopening holds and whether any areas remain restricted. Medford Public Schools’ public site lists the district’s news and calendar information, but the incident details in the reports cited here came from statements provided to news outlets. The district had not publicly described the underlying pipe failure, a repair invoice, a timetable for permanent work or any additional safety measures in the material reviewed by NorthEast News. Those details would be needed to determine whether Monday was a one-time plumbing failure or part of a larger facilities problem.

The confirmed sequence is therefore limited but consequential: a sewer odor was detected in one hallway, firefighters responded, the high school was evacuated, students and staff were dismissed, a drain contractor located the backup, and the district announced a Tuesday return. Families should rely on any direct Medford Public Schools notice for last-minute changes to classes, buses, athletics or after-school programs. Until officials release more technical information, the reopening announcement is the operative update, while the cause and any lasting repairs remain questions for the district and city to document.
